question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, which two types of skins supplied the ashes used in the Fanti people's traditional soap preparation?
reference_answer: The ashes came from banana skins and plantain skins.
supporting_passage:
In West Central Africa,
moreover, the natives, especially the Fanti race, have been accustomed
to wash themselves with soap prepared by mixing crude palm oil and water
with the ashes of banana and plantain skins.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, where and at what stage was H. Jackson's patented laundry detergent prepared?
reference_answer: It was prepared in the wash-tub at the time of use.
supporting_passage:
This detergent is prepared in
the wash-tub at the time of use, and it is claimed that goods are
cleansed by merely immersing them in this solution for a short time and
rinsing in fresh water.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what two differences from crystal formation did Krafft's later research describe for solutions that become gelatinous on cooling, in terms of molecular movement and structural arrangement?
reference_answer: The molecules or molecular aggregates move much more slowly than molecules in crystal formation, while still having a definite structure arranged differently from that of a crystal.
required_key_points: molecules or molecular aggregates move much more slowly than in crystal formation
a definite structure exists but is arranged differently from a crystal
supporting_passage:
In the light of their more recent work,
the molecules, or definite aggregates of molecules, of solutions which
become gelatinous on cooling move much more slowly than the molecules in
the formation of a crystal, but there is a definite structure, although
arranged differently to that of a crystal.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, besides caustic soda, which two named alcohols and which additional substance do the authors report as slowing the hydrolysis of soap?
reference_answer: They name ethyl alcohol, amyl alcohol, and glycerol.
supporting_passage:
Caustic soda exerts a marked retarding
effect on the hydrolysis, as do also ethyl and amyl alcohols and
glycerol.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, which two oily materials did Hillyer's N/10 experiments show were emulsified by the soap solution but not by the alkali solution?
reference_answer: An oil from which all acidity had been removed and kerosene were emulsified by the soap solution but not by the alkali solution.
required_key_points: oil from which all acidity had been removed
supporting_passage:
Experiments by Hillyer (_loc. cit._) show, however, that while N/10
solution of alkali will readily emulsify a cotton-seed oil containing
free acidity, no emulsion is produced with an oil from which all the
acidity has been removed, or with kerosene, whereas a N/10 solution of
sodium oleate will readily give an emulsion with either, thus proving
that the emulsification is due to the soap itself, and not to the
alkali.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, why do the authors say sodium and potassium rosin salts fall outside their definitions of soap yet can still be treated as legitimate soap ingredients?
reference_answer: Rosin's acid constituents are aromatic, excluding its salts from the definitions, but the resinates have properties analogous to true soap.
required_key_points: the acid constituents of rosin are aromatic
rosin salts have properties analogous to true soap
supporting_passage:
Neither of the definitions given above includes the sodium and potassium
salts of rosin, commonly called rosin soap, for the acid constituents of
rosin have been shown to be aromatic, but in view of the analogous
properties of these resinates to true soap, they are generally regarded
as legitimate constituents of soap, having been used in Great Britain
since 1827, and receiving legislative sanction in Holland in 1875.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what specific example do the authors use to argue that viscosity has little influence on emulsification, including the solution and its strength, the viscosity comparison, and its emulsifying performance?
reference_answer: A 1 per cent. solution of sodium oleate has a viscosity very little different from pure water yet is an excellent emulsifying agent.
required_key_points: 1 per cent. solution of sodium oleate
viscosity very little different from that of pure water
supporting_passage:
So far as viscosity is concerned,
this can have but little influence, for a 1 per cent. solution of sodium
oleate, which has a viscosity very little different from that of pure
water, is an excellent emulsifying agent.
